extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of physical science and philosophy of science (scientists, philosophers, advanced students interested in foundations of physics)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and prescribing how 'matter' and 'motion' should be defined and used within scientific method, distinguishing between perceptual data (sense-impressions) and conceptual constructs (geometrical ideals). The chapter offers methodological canons for forming scientific definitions and warns against metaphysical projections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify sphere (perceptual vs conceptual) when asking scientific questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Settle whether questions such as 'What moves?', 'Why does it move?', and 'How does it move?' are being asked of the conceptual sphere (scientific symbols, geometrical ideals) or of the perceptual sphere (sense-impressions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If asked of the conceptual sphere, answers are straightforward (points, rigid bodies, strainable media — geometric concepts). If asked of the perceptual sphere, such questions are often illegitimate or unanswerable because motion is not a reality of perception; perceptual experience affords only change of sense-impressions. Restate or redirect questions into the correct sphere before attempting answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish change (perceptual) from motion (conceptual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat 'change' as the proper term for what occurs in perception (sense-impressions vary, dissolve, form new groups), and 'motion' as a conceptual description applicable to geometrical ideals in conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'motion' only as a conceptual tool to symbolise sequences of perceptions; avoid asserting motion as a direct phenomenal (perceptual) fact. Example: in perception objects appear/disappear/reappear (change), whereas motion describes conceptual displacements in absolute time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ascribe phenomenal existence to concepts without perceptual evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental canon: to no concept, however valuable for describing perceptions, ought phenomenal existence be ascribed until its perceptual equivalent has actually been disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid projecting conceptual mechanisms (e.g., molecules, atoms, other unobserved geometric constructs) into perception as if they were phenomenal realities. Disregarding this canon leads to antinomies and conflicts of rules (examples: postulating atoms/molecules as literally occupying perceptual space or attributing reality to geometrical ideals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical definitions must accord with psychological (perceptual) experience
rubrics_metrics.description: A physical statement or definition should be examined for consistency with psychological experience; scientific statements are not fully satisfactory if they contradict how phenomena present themselves to perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe and question authoritative statements (e.g., definitions by Kelvin, Tait, Clerk-Maxwell) to see whether terms like 'matter' or 'force' refer to sense-impressions or to metaphysical postulates. For instance, if 'force' is asserted as a 'direct object of sense', clarify whether it is experienced as a sense-impression (e.g., muscular sense) or implied metaphysically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphysical 'thing-in-itself' explanations in science
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject as unscientific the use of unknowable metaphysical entities (a 'substratum' or 'thing-in-itself') as causes behind sense-impressions; such entities are meaningless for empirical science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer classificatory, operational accounts (grouping sense-impressions) rather than postulating unknowable causes behind perception. Example critique: defining matter as an unknowable cause of sensations is as idle as invoking supernatural explanations; it should be discarded in scientific exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'matter' operationally as groups of sense-impressions (material sense-impressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For scientific classification it is useful to term particular recurring, more-or-less permanent groups of sense-impressions 'material sense-impressions' and treat 'matter' as the label for such groups rather than as an unknowable substrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operational classification is scientifically valuable but must not be conflated with treating matter as the moving thing in perception. Be explicit about what is being classified (sense-impressions) and avoid slipping back into metaphysical posits. The text references J.S. Mill's 'permanent possibility of sensation' as a similar move.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify whether 'space' in definitions is perceptual or conceptual
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining matter (e.g., 'matter is whatever can occupy space'), explicitly state whether 'space' refers to conceptual (geometrical) space or to the perceptual mode by which we distinguish coexisting sense-impression groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 'space' is taken as conceptual, the definition would reduce matter to geometrical forms (undesirable). If 'space' is taken as perceptual-mode, then only groups of sense-impressions occupy space. Failure to specify this leads to confusion between conception and perception and to unjustified projection of conceptual volumes into the phenomenal world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat impenetrability and hardness as relative perceptual properties, not absolute metaphysical attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties like impenetrability and hardness denote classes of sense-impressions and are often relative (one thing impenetrable relative to another) rather than absolute attributes of 'matter'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assert absolute impenetrability (e.g., glass is impenetrable to birds but penetrable to light); specify the domain of interaction. Be cautious about invoking atoms' impenetrability as an absolute explanatory law without acknowledging alternative hypotheses that could explain observed regularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sameness of perceived object does not imply sameness of underlying substratum
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptual sameness (recurrence of the same group of sense-impressions) does not logically require an identical, persistent substratum underlying them; permanence may lie in the grouping rather than in an enduring imperceptible entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the wave-on-water analogy: a wave retains its form though its substratum (water particles) changes; similarly, the identity of a material object in perception may be maintained by grouping rules, not by an unchanged atomistic substratum. Avoid inferring indestructible/impermeable individuals unless such hypotheses are the best explanatory devices for observed phenomena.
